title: One membrane decides it: prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells in contact

objectives.statement: Use the nuclear-envelope test as the working criterion it is: classify the cells this lesson describes from whether a membrane encloses their DNA, sort further statements into those that follow from that answer, those it only makes possible, those that are tendencies with exceptions, and those it does not license, and state what the test does not settle, group membership being decided by ancestry.

Calculate surface area per unit volume and diffusion crossing time for a stated cell geometry, express the difference between two cells as a factor, and explain why a change in size changes those two consequences by different amounts and what each one constrains.

Explain what enclosing DNA in a nuclear envelope makes possible for the control of gene expression and what it costs, and use that trade-off together with genome size and division machinery to account for observed generation times in a gut bacterium, a human cell, and a slow-growing prokaryote.

scenes.title: Two ways to build a cell, in contact all day
How much membrane, and how long to cross
A room of its own, and the rent it charges
Older, simpler, lesser: three words that do not follow
Four problems, and less help each time
Why one culture reads out overnight and another takes six weeks
Clinical wrap-up: the drug that can tell your cells from theirs
